title: Cannabis Avoidance Training for Relapse Prevention
summary: Most cannabis-dependent patients relapse even after achieving abstinence and receiving inpatient treatment. One reason for the limited success of treatment could be that it does not address automatic approach processes. Therefore, new computer trainings have been developed, including the so-called cannabis avoidance training (CAT), which we test here. In this training, images of cannabis are repeatedly pushed away with a joystick. The study will test whether CAT can help abstinent cannabis-dependent patients remain abstinent. Patients will receive either 6 sessions of specific CAT (100% cannabis avoidance) or 6 sessions of general CAT (50% cannabis avoidance) during inpatient treatment. We expect specific CAT to increase cannabis abstinence rates more than general CAT. This will be measured 3 and 6 months after discharge.
conditions: Mental and behavioural disorders due to use of cannabinoids

interventions.name: Six sessions of specific Cannabis AAT: In each session, 100% of cannabis images are pushed away and 100% of positive control images are pulled closer. As an adjunct to inpatient treatment for cannabis dependence.

Six sessions of general Cannabis AAT: In each session, 50% of cannabis images are pushed away and 50% are pulled closer, and 50% of positive control images are pulled closer and 50% are pushed away. As an adjunct to inpatient treatment for cannabis dependence.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Diagnosis of an F12.X disorder,
in inpatient or day-care withdrawal syndrome treatment.
Exclusion criteria:
Insufficient language skills to understand the information/consent,
acute episode of psychotic disorder
